# Page Transcriber

You turn **specific PDF pages into faithful LaTeX**, one self-contained file per

more, do the first 5, and report the rest as a follow-up range to call again —
do not try to do them all in one pass (accuracy collapses on long ranges).

## Steps

1. **Render the pages to images** (so you can *see* them — this is what makes it
   vision, not OCR). Use poppler, already installed:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p references/<slug>/pages
   pdftoppm -png -r 200 -f <first> -l <last> references/<slug>/<file>.pdf references/<slug>/pages/page
   # produces references/<slug>/pages/page-<N>.png ; rename to zero-padded page-NNNN.png
   ```

2. **Look at each page image** with your vision capability (open/read the PNG).
   Read the actual rendered page — the math, the prose, the figures' captions.
   Do **not** shell out to an OCR tool and do **not** transcribe from the PDF's
   embedded text layer; transcribe from what you see.

3. **Write faithful LaTeX for that page.** Reproduce the mathematics exactly:
   theorem/definition/proof environments, displayed and inline math, numbering as
   printed. Keep prose that carries mathematical meaning; you may drop running
   headers/footers and page numbers. Mark anything genuinely illegible with
   `% [illegible]` rather than inventing it. **Do not fabricate** content you
   cannot read.

Write one file per page to `references/<slug>/tex/page-NNNN.tex`, zero-padded,

   264	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1(-D))\) consisting of differentials that vanish at
   265	  \(Q\).  Outside the common zero locus of a basis of this latter space,
   266	  adding \(Q\) lowers \(h^1\) by exactly one.  Starting with the zero
   267	  divisor, for which \(h^1=g\), and repeating this argument \(r\) times
   268	  gives a dense open subset of \(C^r\) on which
   269	  \(h^1(P_1+\cdots+P_r)=g-r\).  Riemann--Roch then gives
   270	  \[
   271	    h^0(P_1+\cdots+P_r)
   272	      =r+1-g+(g-r)=1.
   273	  \]
   274	  Intersecting its finitely many translates under \(S_r\) gives a dense
   275	  symmetric open with the same property.  Its image in the finite quotient
   276	  \(C^{(r)}\) is the complement of the image of its closed invariant
   277	  complement, hence is open and dense.
   278	  Since the fibre of \(f^{(r)}\) through \(D\) is \(|D|\), it is a single
   279	  point there.
   280	\end{proof}
   281	
   282	\begin{lemma}
   283	  [One-forms pulled back by the Abel--Jacobi map]
   284	  \label{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}
   285	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0108}
   286	  \uses{lem:abel_jacobi_morphism, thm:pic0_tangent_space_iso}
   287	
   288	  Pullback by \(\iota_{P_0}\) is an isomorphism
   289	  \[
   290	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^0(C,\Omega_C^1).
   291	  \]
   292	\end{lemma}
   293	
   294	\begin{proof}
   295	  Translation identifies global one-forms on the smooth group scheme \(J\)
   296	  with the cotangent space at its identity.  The tangent-space description
   297	  of \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) identifies the tangent space at the identity with
   298	  \(H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)\), whose dual is
   299	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\) by Serre duality.  Under these identifications, the
   300	  differential of the moduli class
   301	  \(Q\mapsto[\mathcal O_C(Q-P_0)]\) is the boundary class of the moving
   302	  point; its dual is evaluation of differentials.  Thus the induced map on
   303	  cotangent spaces, and hence the displayed pullback map, is the identity
   304	  under the canonical identifications.
   305	\end{proof}
   306	
   307	\begin{proposition}
   308	  [Differentials on a symmetric power]
   309	  \label{prop:symmetric_product_differentials}
   310	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0108, abelian-varieties:page-0109}
   311	  \uses{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms, def:symmetric_power_curve}
   312	
   313	  Pullback by \(f^{(r)}\) is an isomorphism
   314	  \[
   315	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\xrightarrow{\sim}
   316	    H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega_{C^{(r)}}^1).
   317	  \]
   318	  Under the canonical identification of either side with
   319	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\), the form corresponding to \(\omega\) vanishes at
   320	  an effective divisor \(D\) if and only if
   321	  \(\operatorname{div}(\omega)\ge D\).
   322	\end{proposition}
   323	
   324	\begin{proof}
   325	  A global one-form on \(C^r\) is a sum of pullbacks from the factors.
   326	  Hence the invariant forms are exactly
   327	  \(\sum_i p_i^*\omega\), with \(\omega\in H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\).
   328	  The quotient map \(\pi_r\) is separable, so pullback embeds
   329	  \(H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega^1)\) into this invariant subspace.  The composite
   330	  \[
   331	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\longrightarrow H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega^1)
   332	      \longrightarrow H^0(C^r,\Omega^1)^{S_r}
   333	  \]
   334	  is the pullback by the sum of the \(r\) copies of the Abel--Jacobi map.
   335	  By \cref{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}, it sends a form to
   336	  \(\sum_i p_i^*\omega\) and is an isomorphism.  Consequently both arrows
   337	  in the display are isomorphisms.
   338	
   339	  It remains to identify vanishing at a divisor.  First take \(D=rQ\),
   340	  choose a parameter \(X\) at \(Q\), and write
   341	  \(\omega=(a_0+a_1X+\cdots)dX\).  In the completed local ring of
   342	  \(C^{(r)}\) at \(D\), use the elementary symmetric functions
   343	  \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r\) in local parameters
   344	  \(X_1,\ldots,X_r\), and put
   345	  \(\tau_j=\sum_iX_i^j,dX_i\).  The identities
   346	  \[
   347	    \sigma_m\tau_0-\sigma_{m-1}\tau_1+\cdots+(-1)^m\tau_m
   348	      =d\sigma_{m+1}
   349	      \qquad(0\le m<r)
   350	  \]
   351	  show that \(\tau_0,\ldots,\tau_{r-1}\) form a basis of the cotangent
   352	  module.  The descended form is \(\sum_{j\ge0}a_j\tau_j\), so it
   353	  vanishes at \(D\) exactly when
   354	  \(a_0=\cdots=a_{r-1}=0\), equivalently when
   355	  \(\operatorname{ord}_Q(\omega)\ge r\).  The same calculation in the
   356	  completed local product for
   357	  \(D=\sum_Q n_QQ\) gives the stated criterion.
   358	\end{proof}
   359	
   360	\begin{lemma}
   361	  [Tangent sequence of the canonical symmetric-power map]
   362	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_tangent_exact}
   363	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107, abelian-varieties:page-0109}
   364	  \uses{prop:symmetric_product_differentials}
   365	
   366	  Let \(F=|D|\) be the fibre of \(f^{(r)}\) through an effective divisor
   367	  \(D\), and put \(a=f^{(r)}(D)\).  The sequence
   368	  \[
   369	    0\longrightarrow T_DF\longrightarrow T_DC^{(r)}
   370	      \xrightarrow{\,d f^{(r)}_D\,}T_aJ
   371	  \]
   372	  is exact.  In particular, if \(h^0(D)=1\), then
   373	  \(d f^{(r)}_D\) is injective.
   374	\end{lemma}
   375	
   376	\begin{proof}
   377	  The first arrow is injective because the fibre is a closed subscheme, and
   378	  its image lies in the kernel because \(f^{(r)}\) is constant on the
   379	  fibre.  By \cref{prop:symmetric_product_differentials}, the annihilator
   380	  in \(T_aJ^\vee\) of the image of \(d f^{(r)}_D\) is
   381	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1(-D))\).  Serre duality therefore gives
   382	  \[
   383	    \dim\ker(d f^{(r)}_D)=r-g+h^1(D).
   384	  \]
   385	  The fibre \(F\) is the projective space of effective divisors in the
   386	  complete linear system, so it is smooth of dimension \(h^0(D)-1\).
   387	  Thus \(\dim T_DF=\dim|D|=h^0(D)-1\), and Riemann--Roch says
   388	  \(h^0(D)-1=r-g+h^1(D)\).  The included subspaces have the same
   389	  dimension, proving exactness.  When \(h^0(D)=1\), this dimension is zero.
   390	\end{proof}
   391	
   392	\begin{lemma}
   393	  [Birationality of the canonical map]
   394	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian}
   395	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107, abelian-varieties:page-0108,
   396	    abelian-varieties:page-0109}
   397	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.symmetricPowerToJacobian}
   398	  \uses{lem:abel_jacobi_morphism, def:symmetric_power_curve,
   399	    lem:jacobian_scheme_grpObj, lem:symmetric_product_general_divisor,
   400	    lem:symmetric_product_tangent_exact}
   401	
   402	  For \(1\le r\le g\), the morphism
   403	  \[
   404	    f^{(r)}\colon C^{(r)}\longrightarrow W^r
   405	  \]
   406	  is birational.  In particular, \(W^g=J\), and
   407	  \(f^{(g)}\colon C^{(g)}\to J\) is a birational surjective morphism.
   408	\end{lemma}
   409	
   410	\begin{proof}
   411	  By \cref{lem:symmetric_product_general_divisor}, the map is injective on
   412	  geometric points over a dense open subset.  Thus the induced extension
   413	  of function fields has separable degree one.  In positive characteristic
   414	  this still leaves open the possibility of a nontrivial purely
   415	  inseparable extension.  Choose \(D\) in that open.  Then \(h^0(D)=1\),
   416	  so \cref{lem:symmetric_product_tangent_exact} makes
   417	  \(d f^{(r)}_D\) injective.  Since source and image both have dimension
   418	  \(r\), the differential has full rank, and the function-field extension
   419	  is generically separable.  Its inseparable degree is therefore also one.
   420	  The function fields of \(C^{(r)}\) and \(W^r\) are equal, proving
   421	  birationality.
   422	
   423	  For \(r=g\), the image \(W^g\) is a closed irreducible subvariety of the
   424	  irreducible variety \(J\) and has dimension \(g=\dim J\).  Hence
   425	  \(W^g=J\).  Surjectivity follows because \(C^{(g)}\) is proper and its
   426	  image is exactly \(W^g\).
   427	\end{proof}
   428	
   429	\section{Descent and the universal property}
   430	\label{sec:albaneseup_descent}
   431	
   432	\begin{lemma}
   433	  [Descent through the birational symmetric power]
   434	  \label{lem:descent_through_birational_sigma}
   435	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   436	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.descentThroughBirationalSigma}
   437	  \uses{lem:symmetric_product_av_map, lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian,
   438	    thm:rational_map_to_av_extends}
   439	
   440	  Let \(A\) be an abelian variety and let
   441	  \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) be pointed at \(P_0\).  There is a unique
   442	  regular morphism \(\psi\colon J\to A\) such that
   443	  \[
   444	    \varphi^{(g)}=\psi\circ f^{(g)}.
   445	  \]
   446	\end{lemma}
   447	
   448	\begin{proof}
   449	  On dense opens \(U\subseteq C^{(g)}\) and \(V\subseteq J\), the map
   450	  \(f^{(g)}|_U\colon U\to V\) is an isomorphism.  Thus
   451	  \(\varphi^{(g)}|_U\circ(f^{(g)}|_U)^{-1}\) defines a rational map
   452	  \(J\dashrightarrow A\).  The Jacobian is smooth and \(A\) is an abelian
   453	  variety, so \cref{thm:rational_map_to_av_extends} extends this rational
   454	  map uniquely to a regular morphism \(\psi\colon J\to A\).  The two
   455	  morphisms \(\varphi^{(g)}\) and \(\psi\circ f^{(g)}\) agree on the dense
   456	  open \(U\); since \(C^{(g)}\) is reduced and \(A\) is separated, they
   457	  agree everywhere.  The same dense-open agreement proves uniqueness.
   458	\end{proof}
   459	
   460	\begin{lemma}
   461	  [Equivalence of the two factorisation equations]
   462	  \label{lem:albanese_eq_iff_symmetricPower_eq}
   463	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   464	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.albanese_eq_iff_symmetricPower_eq}
   465	  \uses{lem:abel_jacobi_morphism, lem:symmetric_product_av_map,
   466	    lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian, lem:av_regular_map_is_hom}
   467	
   468	  Let \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) satisfy \(\varphi(P_0)=0_A\).  For every
   469	  regular morphism \(\psi\colon J\to A\),
   470	  \[
   471	    \varphi=\psi\circ\iota_{P_0}
   472	      \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   473	    \varphi^{(g)}=\psi\circ f^{(g)}.
   474	  \]
   475	\end{lemma}
   476	
   477	\begin{proof}
   478	  Suppose first that \(\varphi=\psi\circ\iota_{P_0}\).  Evaluating at
   479	  \(P_0\) gives \(\psi(0_J)=0_A\), so
   480	  \cref{lem:av_regular_map_is_hom} shows that \(\psi\) is a homomorphism.
   481	  Pulling both sides of the desired symmetric-power equation back to
   482	  \(C^g\), both send \((P_1,\ldots,P_g)\) to
   483	  \(\sum_i\psi(\iota_{P_0}(P_i))\).  Surjectivity of
   484	  \(\pi_g\colon C^g\to C^{(g)}\) gives the equation on \(C^{(g)}\).
   485	
   486	  Conversely, compose the symmetric-power equation with
   487	  \[
   488	    C\longrightarrow C^{(g)},\qquad
   489	    Q\longmapsto Q+(g-1)P_0.
   490	  \]
   491	  On the left this gives
   492	  \(\varphi(Q)+(g-1)\varphi(P_0)=\varphi(Q)\), while on the right it gives
   493	  \(\psi(\iota_{P_0}(Q))\).  Hence
   494	  \(\varphi=\psi\circ\iota_{P_0}\).
   495	\end{proof}
   496	
   497	\begin{theorem}
   498	  [Albanese factorisation through \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\)]
   499	  \label{thm:albanese_universal_property}
   500	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   501	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.albanese_universal_property}
   502	  \uses{lem:descent_through_birational_sigma,
   503	    lem:albanese_eq_iff_symmetricPower_eq}
   504	
   505	  For every abelian variety \(A\) and every morphism
   506	  \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) with \(\varphi(P_0)=0_A\), there exists a unique
   507	  regular morphism \(\psi\colon J\to A\) such that
   508	  \[
   509	    \varphi=\psi\circ\iota_{P_0}.
   510	  \]
   511	\end{theorem}
   512	
   513	\begin{proof}
   514	  By \cref{lem:descent_through_birational_sigma}, there is a unique
   515	  \(\psi\colon J\to A\) satisfying
   516	  \(\varphi^{(g)}=\psi\circ f^{(g)}\).  The equivalence in
   517	  \cref{lem:albanese_eq_iff_symmetricPower_eq}, applied to every candidate
   518	  morphism, transports both existence and uniqueness to the equation
   519	  \(\varphi=\psi\circ\iota_{P_0}\).
   520	\end{proof}
   521	
   522	\begin{corollary}
   523	  [Albanese universal property]
   524	  \label{cor:albanese_universal_property_homomorphism}
   525	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   526	  \uses{thm:albanese_universal_property, lem:av_regular_map_is_hom,
   527	    lem:abel_jacobi_morphism}
   528	
   529	  In the situation of \cref{thm:albanese_universal_property}, the unique
   530	  factor \(\psi\colon J\to A\) is a homomorphism of group schemes.
   531	  Consequently \(\iota_{P_0}\) is initial among pointed morphisms from
   532	  \(C\) to abelian varieties.
   533	\end{corollary}
   534	
   535	\begin{proof}
   536	  Since \(\iota_{P_0}(P_0)=0_J\) and \(\varphi(P_0)=0_A\), the
   537	  factorisation gives \(\psi(0_J)=0_A\).  The pointed rigidity theorem
   538	  \cref{lem:av_regular_map_is_hom} therefore makes \(\psi\) a group
   539	  homomorphism.  Uniqueness among all regular factors implies uniqueness
   540	  among homomorphisms.
   541	\end{proof}

% source: J. S. Milne, "Abelian Varieties" (course notes), v2.00, 2008, www.jmilne.org
% pdf_page: 0100
% doc_page: 94 (Chapter III, Section 3, "The symmetric powers of a curve"; Propositions 3.1 and 3.2)

% [running head: CHAPTER III. JACOBIAN VARIETIES, page 94]

\section*{3 \quad The symmetric powers of a curve}

Both in order to understand the structure of the Jacobian, and as an aid in
its construction, we shall need to study the symmetric powers of $C$.

For any variety $V$, the symmetric group $S_r$ on $r$ letters acts on the
product of $r$ copies $V^r$ of $V$ by permuting the factors, and we want to
define the $r$th symmetric power $V^{(r)}$ of $V$ to be the quotient
$S_r \backslash V^r$. The next proposition demonstrates the existence of
$V^{(r)}$ and lists its main properties.

A morphism $\varphi \colon V^r \to T$ is said to be \textit{symmetric} if
$\varphi\sigma = \varphi$ for all $\sigma$ in $S_r$.

\paragraph{Proposition 3.1.}
\textit{Let $V$ be a variety over $k$. Then there exists a variety $V^{(r)}$
and a symmetric morphism $\pi \colon V^r \to V^{(r)}$ having the following
properties:}

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \textit{as a topological space, $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ is the quotient
of $V^r$ by $S_r$;}
\item[(b)] \textit{for any open affine subset $U$ of $V$, $U^{(r)}$ is an
open affine subset of $V^{(r)}$ and}
\[
  \Gamma(U^{(r)}, \mathcal{O}_{V^{(r)}})
  = \Gamma(U^r, \mathcal{O}_{V^r})^{S_r}
\]
\textit{(set of elements fixed by the action of $S_r$).}
\end{enumerate}

\textit{The pair $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ has the following universal property:
every symmetric $k$-morphism $\varphi \colon V^r \to T$ factors uniquely
through $\pi$.}

\textit{The map $\pi$ is finite, surjective, and separable.}

\paragraph{Proof.}
If $V$ is affine, say $V = \operatorname{Specm}(A)$, define $V^{(r)}$ to be
$\operatorname{Specm}((A \otimes_k \cdots \otimes_k A)^{S_r})$. In the
general case, write $V$ as a union $\bigcup U_i$ of open affines, and construct
$V$ by patching together the $U_i^{(r)}$. See Mumford 1970, II, \S 7, p66,
and III, \S 11, p112, for the details. \hfill $\square$

The pair $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ is uniquely determined up to a unique isomorphism
by its universal property. It is called the $r$th \textit{symmetric power} of
$V$.

\paragraph{Proposition 3.2.}
\textit{The symmetric power $C^{(r)}$ of a nonsingular curve is nonsingular.}

\paragraph{Proof.}
We may assume that $k$ is algebraically closed. The most likely candidate for
a singular point on $C^{(r)}$ is the image $Q$ of a fixed point
$(P, \ldots, P)$ of $S_r$ on $C^r$, where $P$ is a closed point of $C$. The
completion $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_P$ of the local ring at $P$ is isomorphic to
$k[[X]]$, and so
\[
  \widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{(P,\ldots,P)}
  \approx k[[X]] \widehat{\otimes} \cdots \widehat{\otimes} k[[X]]
  \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]].
\]
It follows that
$\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_Q \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]^{S_r}$, where $S_r$
acts by permuting the variables. The fundamental theorem on symmetric
functions says that, over any ring, a symmetric polynomial can be expressed
as a polynomial in the elementary symmetric functions
$\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r$. This implies that
\[
  k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]^{S_r} = k[[\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r]],
\]
which is regular, and so $Q$ is nonsingular.

For a general point $Q = \pi(P, P, \ldots, P', \ldots)$ with $P$ occurring
$r'$ times, $P'$ occurring $r''$ times, and so on,
\[
  \widehat{\mathcal{O}}_Q
  \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_{r'}]]^{S_{r'}} \widehat{\otimes}
  k[[X_1, \ldots, X_{r''}]]^{S_{r''}} \widehat{\otimes} \cdots,
\]
which the same argument shows to be regular. \hfill $\square$
